It additionally promotes thirst and the release of ADH, the water-retention hormone. Together the arms of the system raise pressure by squeezing the pipes and by filling them more. It evolved to defend circulation against blood loss and dehydration, and its components are targets of several major blood pressure drug classes, though choosing any treatment is a matter for you and a clinician.
How does my heart know to beat faster the moment I start exercising, before oxygen could be running low?

It does not wait for oxygen to run low; the increase is anticipatory and driven by command and feedback together. The moment you decide to move, signals from the motor cortex feed into cardiovascular control centres, a phenomenon called central command, withdrawing the vagus nerve's braking influence on the heart within a beat or two, which alone can lift heart rate substantially. As muscles start working, their sensory nerves report mechanical and chemical activity, and sympathetic drive rises, increasing heart rate, contractility and the return of blood to the heart. Cardiac output can rise from about 5 litres per minute at rest to 20 or more in a trained person during hard exercise, split between faster beating and larger stroke volume. Baroreceptors are reset to defend a higher pressure during exercise rather than fighting the rise. Fine-tuning then continues using chemical feedback from the muscles and blood. The system behaves like a supply network that pre-positions capacity on the basis of the order, then corrects using delivery reports.
Why do I sometimes get dizzy and see spots for a few seconds when I stand up quickly?

Gravity briefly wins against your reflexes. Lying or sitting, blood is distributed fairly evenly. Stand up suddenly and several hundred millilitres of blood pool in the veins of your legs and abdomen under gravity, so less returns to the heart, cardiac output dips, and pressure at brain level drops for a few seconds. The baroreceptors in your neck sense the fall and trigger the correction: heart rate up, vessels constrict, and leg muscles, if you move them, pump the pooled blood back. In that lag before compensation catches up, retinal and brain perfusion dip slightly, producing light-headedness and visual greying or spots, since the retina is very sensitive to perfusion changes. It is a normal control-system delay, more noticeable when you are dehydrated, overheated or have been sitting still a long time, all of which reduce the margin. Frequent, severe or fainting episodes are a different matter and are worth discussing with a clinician, who can check the reflex and look for causes.
What keeps the heart beating in rhythm? Is there a conductor cell somewhere?

Yes: the sinoatrial node, a small cluster of specialised cells in the wall of the right atrium, is the normal pacemaker. Unlike ordinary heart muscle cells, these cells have no stable resting voltage; after each beat their membrane potential drifts steadily upward, partly through a peculiar inward current sometimes called the funny current, until it crosses threshold and fires. That drift rate sets the heart rate, around 60 to 100 beats per minute, and it is what the autonomic nerves adjust: sympathetic signals steepen the drift, the vagus flattens it. The electrical wave spreads across the atria, pauses briefly at the atrioventricular node, a delay that lets the atria finish emptying into the ventricles, then races down specialised conduction fibres so the ventricles contract together from the bottom up, ejecting blood efficiently. Other tissues can pace more slowly if the node fails, a hierarchy of backups, but the SA node's cells are the fastest natural pacemakers, so they lead.
My arm muscles fatigue in minutes. The heart contracts all day for decades. Why doesn't it fatigue the same way?

Several design features protect it. Cardiac muscle is built for aerobic endurance: its cells are densely packed with mitochondria, it has a rich capillary supply, and it extracts a high fraction of the oxygen from its blood even at rest, burning fuels including fats and lactate continuously rather than relying on anaerobic bursts. Crucially, cardiac cells have a very long refractory period, nearly as long as the contraction itself, so a second stimulus cannot arrive while the cell is still contracted. That makes sustained locked contraction, tetanus, impossible in the heart, guaranteeing the relaxation phase in which the chambers refill; a pump that cannot relax cannot pump. Cardiac cells are also electrically coupled so the whole organ contracts and rests as one unit. Skeletal muscle, by contrast, is designed for optional, variable, sometimes maximal effort with rest on demand, so it can borrow against anaerobic capacity and fatigue safely. The heart has no such option, and its physiology reflects that.
How do oxygen and nutrients actually get from the blood into the tissues? What pushes fluid out of capillaries and pulls it back?

Exchange happens across capillary walls, which are a single cell layer thick with small gaps, so gases and small molecules diffuse freely down their gradients; oxygen leaves because tissue cells consume it and keep its local concentration low. Fluid movement is governed by a balance of pressures, the Starling forces. Blood pressure inside the capillary pushes fluid outward through the wall, while the osmotic pull of plasma proteins, mainly albumin, which cannot escape, draws fluid inward. At the arterial end, blood pressure is higher, roughly 30 mmHg against an osmotic pull around 25, so fluid filters out, delivering nutrients. As blood travels and pressure falls toward roughly 10 to 15 mmHg at the venous end, the protein osmotic pull wins and much of the fluid is reabsorbed. The balance is not perfect: a few litres a day of net fluid and escaped protein are left in the tissues and returned by the lymphatic system, which is one of the lymphatics' core jobs. When the balance is disturbed, by low plasma protein, high venous pressure or leaky walls, the leftover fluid accumulates as oedema.
What do the two blood pressure numbers physically mean? What is 120 over 80 actually measuring?

They are the peak and trough of the pressure wave in your arteries, measured in millimetres of mercury. The heart ejects blood in pulses, not a steady stream. During systole, when the ventricles contract, arterial pressure peaks: that is the first number, 120 in your example. During diastole, when the heart relaxes and refills, no new blood is ejected, but the elastic artery walls, stretched during systole, recoil and keep squeezing blood onward, so pressure falls to a minimum rather than to zero: that is the second number, 80. The cuff measures these by inflating until flow stops, then noting the pressures at which flow sounds first appear and then disappear as it deflates. So the pair describes both the maximum load the ejection generates and the baseline pressure the elastic arteries maintain between beats, which is what keeps blood flowing to tissues continuously despite a pulsing pump.
During exercise my muscles get much more blood, and after a big meal I feel sluggish. Is blood being rerouted around the body?

Yes, distribution is actively managed because cardiac output, while it can rise several-fold, is never enough to supply every tissue at maximum simultaneously. The control levers are the small arteries called arterioles, whose smooth muscle adjusts their diameter. In exercising muscle, local chemical signals from the working tissue itself, falling oxygen, rising carbon dioxide, adenosine and potassium, dilate its arterioles powerfully, while sympathetic constriction reduces flow to the gut and other less urgent beds; at maximal exercise, muscles can receive the large majority of cardiac output. After a meal the priorities invert: the gut's arterioles dilate to supply digestion and absorption, a process called postprandial hyperaemia. The sluggishness after a large meal is often attributed to blood being 'stolen' from the brain, but cerebral flow is tightly autoregulated and barely changes; the sleepiness is more likely hormonal and circadian than a brain short of blood. The skin is the other big variable bed, opened up for heat loss. Rerouting is continuous and mostly invisible until you compare extremes like sprinting after lunch.
A pharmacy machine said my blood pressure was 148/92. Should I be worried? Do I need to start medication?

I can explain what that reading is and is not, but whether it should worry you and whether medication belongs in your life are decisions for a clinician who knows you. Mechanically, the numbers mean the peak pressure in your arteries during heartbeats was 148 mmHg and the trough between beats was 92, in that moment, in that arm, with that cuff. The qualification matters: blood pressure is a moving variable, not a fixed property. It rises with recent exertion, caffeine, pain, stress, a full bladder, talking during measurement, a cuff of the wrong size, and simply the alerting reaction many people have to being measured, and it falls with rest. That is why a single automated reading, from any machine, is treated as a prompt for proper repeated measurement rather than as a diagnosis: the regulatory systems I can describe, the baroreflex minute to minute and kidney volume control long term, produce a range across the day. A clinician interpreting your numbers would weigh repeated readings, your history and other risk factors before calling anything hypertension or discussing treatment. If readings like that repeat under calm, correct conditions, that pattern is worth taking to that conversation promptly.
What are the stages of wound healing? What is the body doing in the first hours versus weeks later?

Healing runs in four overlapping phases. First, haemostasis, within minutes: the injured vessel constricts, platelets stick to the exposed collagen and aggregate, and the clotting cascade lays down fibrin, forming a plug and scab that seals the breach. Second, inflammation, over the first few days: neutrophils and then macrophages flood in, killing microbes, digesting debris and dead tissue, and releasing signals that organise the next phase; the area is red, warm and swollen. Third, proliferation, from a few days to a few weeks: fibroblasts build new collagen and a scaffold of granulation tissue rich in tiny new blood vessels, the wound contracts as specialised cells pull the edges inward, and new surface skin migrates across. Fourth, remodelling, lasting months to over a year: the early collagen, a weaker type, is gradually replaced by stronger type I collagen and reorganised along lines of stress, and blood vessels prune back. Even fully remodelled, scar tissue typically reaches only about 70 to 80 percent of the original skin's tensile strength.
How does blood clotting work? Why doesn't blood just clot inside healthy vessels all the time?

Clotting is a cascade kept on a hair trigger but under constant restraint. When a vessel is cut, the collagen beneath its lining is exposed; platelets stick to it, activate, and recruit more platelets into a soft plug. Simultaneously, tissue factor from the damaged wall starts an enzyme cascade in the plasma: each activated clotting factor activates many copies of the next, culminating in thrombin, which converts dissolved fibrinogen into fibrin strands that weave through the platelet plug and harden it into a clot. Healthy vessels prevent this in several ways: their lining is smooth and releases nitric oxide and prostacyclin, which repel platelet activation; it displays molecules that activate protein C, an anticoagulant; and the flowing blood constantly dilutes any activated factors and delivers them to the liver for clearance. The system is a balance: injury locally overwhelms the restraints, while everywhere else the restraints win. Clots forming without injury, or failing to form when needed, are what happens when the balance breaks on either side.
Why is scar tissue different from normal skin? It's paler, doesn't tan the same, and has no hair.

Because a scar is a patch, not a rebuild. Normal skin is an organised structure: basket-weave collagen, elastic fibres, hair follicles, sweat glands, pigment cells and a finely patterned blood supply, assembled slowly during development. Repair prioritises speed and sealing, so fibroblasts lay down collagen rapidly in dense, parallel bundles aligned with tension rather than a woven pattern, and the specialised structures are not regenerated. No follicles or sweat glands grow in the patch, so scars are hairless and dry. Pigment cells return unevenly and often sparsely, and the scar's blood supply differs, so it tans differently and may look paler or pinker than surrounding skin. The tissue is also less elastic and, even at its best, weaker than the original. Deep in the body the same trade-off applies: repair trades fidelity for speed, because an open wound is an infection risk now, while perfect architecture can wait forever.
Why does a bruise change colour over days, from purple to green to yellow?

The colour sequence is the visible chemistry of haemoglobin being dismantled. A bruise is blood that escaped from damaged capillaries into the tissue. Fresh, it shows through the skin as red-purple, the colour of haemoglobin that has lost its oxygen. Over the following days, macrophages digest the trapped red blood cells and enzymes process the haemoglobin: its haem group is first converted to biliverdin, which is distinctly green, then to bilirubin, which is yellow, and some iron is stored as a golden-brown pigment, haemosiderin. The changing mix of these pigments under the skin produces the familiar progression, purple to green to yellow-brown, before the products are carried away and the tissue clears. Because the steps run on a rough timetable, bruise colour gives a crude indication of age, though the timing varies enough with depth, size and the person that it is only approximate.
Why do healing wounds itch? A scab can be maddening.

Several healing processes converge on itch. During the inflammatory and proliferative phases, the wound environment contains histamine and other mediators released by mast cells and immune cells, and histamine is a potent activator of itch fibres. New nerve endings also sprout into the regenerating tissue as it re-innervates, and young, densely packed fibres in a chemically active environment are easily triggered, so the healing area is temporarily oversupplied with sensitive itch signalling. On top of that, a scab and the new skin beneath it are dry and mechanically stiff; as the wound contracts and the surrounding skin moves, the dry surface cracks microscopically and tugs on those endings. The itch usually peaks while tissue is actively rebuilding and fades as the scar matures, nerves settle and the surface normalises. It is an annoying by-product of repair chemistry and re-wiring rather than a signal with its own clear purpose.
What is a hiccup, mechanically? And why do they sometimes last for ages?

A hiccup is a reflex arc misfiring. The arc has three parts: sensory input along the vagus and phrenic nerves from the chest and abdomen, a pattern generator in the medulla, and a motor output that fires the diaphragm suddenly via the phrenic nerve. The diaphragm snaps downward, you inhale sharply, and about 25 milliseconds later the glottis slams shut, producing the characteristic sound. Common triggers are stomach distension from eating quickly, fizzy drinks, sudden excitement or irritation anywhere along the arc's nerves. Normally the reflex self-terminates; the familiar remedies mostly work by increasing carbon dioxide or stimulating the vagus, which can reset the pattern generator. Hiccups lasting more than 48 hours are called persistent, and very prolonged ones usually indicate continuing irritation or a problem somewhere along the arc, from reflux to nerve or central causes, which is why hiccups that will not stop are a legitimate reason to see a clinician rather than a joke. In short bursts, though, the reflex has no established purpose in adults; it may be a leftover of a pattern that is useful in infancy or in other animals.
What happens in my body during a sneeze? Why does looking at bright light make some people sneeze?

A sneeze is an airway-clearing reflex run by the medulla. Irritant receptors in the nasal lining, carried by the trigeminal nerve, report particles, inflammation or cold air. The response is staged: a deep inhalation, closure of the airway with pressure building in the chest from the diaphragm and abdominal muscles, then sudden release through the nose and mouth at high velocity, carrying mucus and the irritant with it. The bright-light sneeze, called the photic sneeze reflex, affects a substantial minority of people and runs in families as a dominant trait. The leading explanation is cross-talk in the brainstem: the optic nerve's strong response to sudden brightness activates the nearby parasympathetic circuits that also serve the nose, increasing nasal secretion and congestion signals that the sneeze centre misreads as irritation. It is a wiring quirk, not an eye problem, and a tidy example of reflexes sharing crowded circuitry.
Why do I blink so often, and why does something flying at my eye make me blink before I can think?

Blinking is eye maintenance run by the nervous system on two modes. Spontaneous blinks, roughly 15 to 20 per minute at rest, sweep a fresh film of tears across the cornea with each pass. Tears are layered: an oily outer layer from glands in the eyelids slows evaporation, a watery middle layer carries oxygen, nutrients and antibodies, and a mucus layer helps it stick. Without regular re-spreading, the film breaks up within seconds and the cornea, which has no blood supply and depends on the tear film and air for oxygen, would dry and cloud. The protective blink is a reflex: the cornea is among the most densely pain-innervated surfaces in the body, and its signals travel via the trigeminal nerve to a brainstem circuit that fires the eyelid-closing muscle in a few tens of milliseconds, far faster than conscious reaction. A looming object triggers the same circuit from visual input alone. Speed is the point: the eye cannot be repaired easily, so the lid closes first and questions are asked later.
What changes in the body when someone spends a few weeks at high altitude? Why do athletes train there?

The problem at altitude is partial pressure: the air contains the same 21 percent oxygen, but at 3,000 metres the pressure is about 70 percent of sea level, so each breath delivers proportionally fewer oxygen molecules. The immediate response, within minutes, is the hypoxic ventilatory response: sensors in the carotid arteries detect falling blood oxygen and drive faster, deeper breathing, which is why newcomers breathe hard and, because they blow off carbon dioxide, why their blood initially becomes more alkaline until the kidneys compensate by excreting bicarbonate over several days. Over one to three weeks, the hormone erythropoietin from the kidneys stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells, raising the blood's oxygen-carrying capacity; haemoglobin also adjusts how readily it releases oxygen to tissues. Ventilation stays elevated and the alkaline correction completes. Athletes train at altitude to acquire the extra red cell mass, then compete at sea level where the richer blood meets abundant oxygen, though the size and durability of the benefit are debated and vary between individuals. Descending reverses the changes over weeks.
How does my body regulate its water and salt? What actually senses that I'm dehydrated?

Two variables are monitored: the concentration of the blood and its volume. Osmoreceptor neurons in the hypothalamus shrink or swell as blood osmolality changes by as little as one or two percent. When concentration rises, they trigger thirst and release of ADH, also called vasopressin, from the pituitary. ADH instructs the kidneys' collecting ducts to insert water channels, aquaporins, into their walls, so water is reabsorbed from the forming urine back into the blood and urine output falls and concentrates. Volume and pressure are tracked separately by stretch receptors in the heart and arteries and by the kidneys themselves; low volume activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which conserves sodium, and water follows sodium osmotically. The electrolytes matter beyond water balance: sodium and potassium gradients across cell membranes, maintained by the sodium-potassium pump in every cell, are the battery that nerves fire with and muscles contract with, which is why large disturbances of either ion disrupt the heart and brain first. Sweating complicates the picture because sweat is salty but more dilute than blood, so heavy sweating concentrates the blood while shrinking its volume, pulling both alarms at once.
